title: Production Reliability Handbook: Observability, SLOs, Deployments, Scaling and DR
summary: Quick revision notes on observing and operating production systems: telemetry, SLO-based alerting, safe releases, autoscaling and disaster recovery with multi-region design.

chapters.title: Observability and Reliability Map
points: Logs, metrics, traces
SLI, SLO, SLA, error budget
Symptom-based alerting
Blue-green, canary, feature flags
Autoscaling
DR: RPO, RTO, multi-region

chapters.title: Logs, Metrics and Traces
points: Definition: logs are timestamped discrete events, metrics are numeric time series aggregated cheaply, traces follow one request across services as spans
Mechanism: a trace ID is generated at the edge and propagated in headers (W3C traceparent); each span records parent ID, duration and status
Comparison: metrics answer 'is something wrong' (cheap, aggregated), traces answer 'where' (per request), logs answer 'why' (highest detail, highest cost)
Example: p99 latency metric spikes, trace shows the payment span slow, log line in that span shows a DB lock timeout; same trace ID links all three
Mistake: high-cardinality labels (user_id, request_id) on metrics explode time series and cost; put them in logs and traces instead; log structured JSON, not free text

chapters.title: SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and Error Budgets
points: Definition: SLI is a measured ratio (good events / valid events); SLO is the internal target for that SLI over a window; SLA is a contract with penalties, looser than the SLO
Mechanism: error budget = 1 - SLO; 99.9% over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of downtime
Comparison: SLI = what you measure, SLO = what you aim for, SLA = what you promise and pay for; SLO is always stricter than SLA
Example: SLO 99.9% of requests under 300 ms succeed; budget burned fast means freeze feature releases and spend time on reliability
Mistake: setting 100% (leaves no budget to ship), measuring server CPU instead of user-facing success, using averages instead of percentiles like p99

chapters.title: Alerting on Symptoms
points: Definition: alert on user-visible symptoms (error rate, latency, availability) not on causes (CPU, memory, a single pod down)
Mechanism: burn-rate alerts compare the current error-budget consumption to the allowed rate; a burn rate of 1 uses exactly the whole budget by window end
Comparison: fast burn (e.g. 14.4x over 1h) pages a human immediately, slow burn (e.g. 1x over 3 days) opens a ticket; use multi-window checks to cut noise
Example: page when 5xx ratio over 5m and 1h both exceed the burn threshold; CPU at 90% with healthy latency creates only a dashboard signal, no page
Mistake: paging on causes causes alert fatigue; every page must be actionable and link to a runbook; no alert should fire for something that self-heals

chapters.title: Safe Releases: Blue-Green, Canary and Feature Flags
points: Definition: blue-green runs two full environments and switches traffic at once; canary shifts a small slice (1%, 5%, 25%, 100%) to the new version; feature flags decouple deploy from release
Mechanism: rollback in blue-green is flipping the router back to the old environment; canary auto-rolls back when SLIs of the canary cohort degrade against baseline
Comparison: blue-green = instant switch and rollback but double the capacity; canary = cheaper and limits blast radius but slower with mixed versions; flags = per-user control with no redeploy
Example: kubectl rollout undo deployment/api reverts a rolling update; a flag 'new_checkout' on for 5% of users, kill switch turns it off in seconds
Mistake: incompatible DB schema changes break rollback (use expand then contract migrations); stale flags pile up as tech debt, remove them after full rollout

chapters.title: Autoscaling, Disaster Recovery and Multi-Region
points: Autoscaling: horizontal adds instances on a metric target (CPU 60%, requests per pod, queue depth); a cooldown or stabilization window stops flapping; set a min for HA and a max for cost control
RPO = max tolerable data loss (time since last good copy); RTO = max tolerable time to restore service; lower values cost more (backups, then replication, then synchronous standby)

Active-passive: the standby is idle or warm, failover is via DNS or a load balancer, simpler and cheaper, with RTO of minutes; active-active: all regions serve traffic, near-zero RTO, but needs conflict resolution and data-consistency design
Example: Kubernetes HPA: kubectl autoscale deployment api --cpu-percent=60 --min=3 --max=20; a payments DB with RPO 0 needs synchronous replication
Mistake: untested DR plans fail; run failover drills, keep backups in a separate region and account, and never scale on lagging metrics when queue depth is available

chapters.title: Reliability Cheat Sheet
points: Signals: metrics say what, traces say where, logs say why; keep metric labels low-cardinality
Budget math: error budget = 1 - SLO; 99.9% is about 43 min per 30 days, 99.99% is about 4.3 min
Alerts: page on symptoms and burn rate, ticket on slow burn, every page has a runbook
Releases: blue-green = instant switch, canary = gradual with auto-rollback, flags = release without deploy
Resilience: RPO is data loss, RTO is downtime; active-passive is cheaper, active-active has the lowest RTO but the hardest consistency; test failover regularly
